Pick the .iso of your Xbox 360 disc, or a folder that has default.xex and LONG2DATA/ (an extracted disc). Only the USA (NTSC-U) version works. The game data is copied into the app (about 6 GB). The executable is checked by SHA-1 right away; \"Verify files\" also checks the archive sizes.

Dragon Burst is the Android port of DBZ Burst Limit Recompiled, a static recompilation of the Xbox 360 game: the game code runs natively, it is not emulated. Based on the PC project by iExplosiveRage:

Thanks to: iExplosiveRage (DBZ Burst Limit Recompiled), NovaPowers (DBZ Budokai 3 HD, whose Android port Dragon Fury this is built on), the ReXGlue SDK team, SDL, libadrenotools (bylaws) and the Turnip/Mesa driver builders (Mr. Purple, StevenMXZ, K11MCH1).
Unofficial, non-commercial fan project. No game files are included: you need your own legal copy. Dragon Ball belongs to Bird Studio/Shueisha, Toei Animation and Bandai Namco.
Game paused while this menu is open.

Resolution, anisotropic filtering and texture packs are in the launcher (they apply when the game opens).
Automatic: they show up when you touch the screen and hide when you use a controller.
The game writes much more to the log. Use it to report a problem; it can cost a little performance.
Every 5 s the log records FPS, GPU time per frame and the GPU clock and load. Light; use it to report stutter.
Copies the full-screen effects straight to the texture, skipping two conversions. Less GPU load.
Also skips copying the effects into the game memory (only the texture is filled). Faster; turn it off if some effect looks wrong.
For graphical glitches with Turnip on Adreno 6xx (e.g. 650). Applied when the game reopens; combine freely. The system driver ignores the TU_DEBUG ones.
No dynamic rendering and stencil export
Game memory in one block (512 MB)
Each pass draws into its own image with no copies between them (less GPU work). Turn off if parts of the image go missing.
Each shader is compiled for the format of its textures, without the extra per-pixel branches and sampling (much faster texturing). Turn off if colors or textures look wrong.
Keeps the 60 FPS game logic but only draws one of every two frames: about half the GPU work. Diagnostic; for smooth play prefer 30 FPS.
What the game is drawn at, then stretched to the screen. 720p is the console resolution; 2K = 1440p (2x), 4K = 2160p (3x).
2K and 4K need much more GPU memory. On Mali GPUs keep 720p or lower.
Off by default, as in the PC version. Turning them on costs GPU (avoid on Mali).
Leave them on unless something looks wrong.

Saves every texture the game loads as .dds in the dump/ folder (Android/data/com.dfdx047.dragonburst/files/textures/dump, or inside the selected pack), already with the right name for a pack. Costs performance: only for making packs.
Export and import, same .zip as the PC version and Xenia

In the game menu (Back + Start > SAVE), Export save creates a .zip listed here; tap the arrow to copy it to Download/. To bring a save from the PC or Xenia, add the .zip here and pick it in Import save (then restart the game).

The PC version\'s LAN / Radmin method: direct UDP (port 59395) on the same network. Host: Create Match. Join: type the host\'s IP, then search a Player Match. Applies when the game opens.
No local network address: connect to Wi-Fi.
Shows the finished frame directly, without the game\'s last full-screen copy (faster, mostly on Mali). Turn off if fades between rounds look wrong.
Native renderer: linear depth by compute
Computes the depth used by the blur, glow and depth-of-field effects straight from the depth buffer, skipping one full-screen pass (faster, mostly on Mali). Turn off if effects look wrong.

In the game, open the menu (Back + Start or the pause button) → System → Capture frames. The next frames are saved and go into Export logs.

Experimental. The game itself runs at 120: its logic follows real time, like the PC version (which offers 120 and 144), so it keeps its normal speed, but the GPU has to draw each frame in under 8.3 ms (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 or newer at 720p). Cutscenes and online were not checked at 120. If it can\'t hold 120, use the interpolated mode.

The game runs at 60 and a generated frame is shown between each two real ones (motion estimation on the GPU, about 1-3 ms per frame). Adds one frame of latency (about 8 ms). Fast moves can show small artifacts at the edges of the characters; the HUD stays sharp.
120 FPS needs a 120 Hz screen; this one goes up to %1$d Hz.
This configuration asks for 120 FPS, but this screen can\'t show it: the game will present at 60 Hz. Pick 30 or 60.
Sets resolution, game effects, frame rate and filters at once, by how heavy they are for the GPU. The renderer optimizations stay on.
Custom settings. Recommended for this device: %1$s
No 1080p: the renderer only multiplies 720p by whole numbers (1080p would be 1.5x). On a 1080p screen, 720p is scaled up and 2K is scaled down (sharper, much heavier).
Below 720p: less sharp, but the GPU draws only %1$d%% of the pixels. AMD FSR 1 (Image) helps the sharpness.
Above 720p the native renderer steps turn off (direct final image, linear depth, contour and glow by compute, passes straight into textures) and the GPU draws %1$dx the pixels.

720p, depth of field and glow, 60 FPS
720p, all effects, 60 FPS, AMD FSR 1 to the screen
2K (1440p), depth of field and motion blur, 60 FPS. Glow and soft filter off (made for 720p)

Skips work that changes nothing: empty draws, resolves that copy the same picture again and resolves nobody reads (mostly with effects off), and the outline of the fighters and its glow drawn by native computes. Turn off if a picture freezes or looks old.
In a fight: freezes it and turns the renderer shortcuts off one at a time, comparing pictures. Shows which one breaks the image and how much each one is worth. Result in Export logs.
Native renderer: passes straight into the texture
Post-processing passes draw straight into the texture they used to be copied to (no copy). Needs a GPU driver with dynamic rendering (Mali; recent Adreno drivers).
